findings.body: The new code builds a shell command string by interpolating user_name and passes it to subprocess.run with shell=True. Because user_name is untrusted input, shell metacharacters such as ;, &, |, $(), or backticks allow arbitrary command execution. The previous implementation used a list argument without a shell, which safely passed user_name as a single argument.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a user_name like "alice; rm -rf /", causing subprocess.run to execute "report --user alice" and then "rm -rf /" in the host shell, leading to remote code execution or data loss.
findings.title: Use a list argument instead of shell=True to prevent command injection

findings.body: datetime.utcnow() returns a timezone-naive datetime and is deprecated. The previous implementation used datetime.now(UTC) to return an aware UTC timestamp. Mixing naive and aware datetimes can cause TypeError on comparison or wrong offsets if the value is interpreted as local time. To fix, restore `from datetime import UTC, datetime` and return a dict with `datetime.now(UTC)`.
findings.failure_scenario: A consumer compares the returned fetched_at against a timezone-aware datetime, raising TypeError, or formats it assuming UTC and gets a local-time offset instead.
findings.title: Use timezone-aware UTC timestamp instead of naive utcnow

findings.body: Treating the user ID as a filesystem path and taking `.name` strips directory components and resolves `..` segments, so an identifier such as `../target-user` becomes `target-user`. The normalized value is then bound to the SQL query, which can return a different user record than the caller intended and bypass authorization decisions. Database identifiers should be used exactly as supplied, not sanitized as file paths. The `from pathlib import PurePath` import will also become unused once the normalization is removed.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a user ID string containing directory separators; `PurePath(...).name` reduces it to the basename, causing the query to return the attacker's chosen user's record.
findings.title: IDOR risk: do not normalize user IDs with PurePath.name

Because the shell parses the string, metacharacters in `user` (spaces, quotes, semicolons, backticks, `$()`, etc.) are interpreted as commands, leading to arbitrary code execution. findings.body: The change introduces `unsafe { std::mem::uninitialized() }` to create a `UserRecord`. `std::mem::uninitialized` is deprecated and undefined behavior for types that are not valid for every bit pattern (e.g., references, enums, bools, or any non-ZST struct). The function then passes the uninitialized value into `UserRecord::merge`, compounding the risk.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who can influence the code path or the contents of `UserRecord` causes the uninitialized memory to be read or interpreted, leading to undefined behavior such as a crash, information disclosure, or control-flow hijacking.
findings.title: Remove use of std::mem::uninitialized for UserRecord

findings.body: The code canonicalizes the candidate path to verify it stays under `root`, but then opens it in a separate step. On Unix, `File::open` follows symlinks, so an attacker who can modify the filesystem between the canonicalization check and the open can replace the allowed path with a symlink to an arbitrary file outside `root`, bypassing the traversal guard and reading sensitive files. Use `O_NOFOLLOW` (via `OpenOptionsExt::custom_flags`) or open relative to a directory file descriptor with `openat` to avoid following symlinks at open time.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker with write access to the reports directory swaps the validated file for a symlink to `/etc/passwd` after `canonicalize` resolves it under `root` but before `File::open` executes; the function then opens the attacker-chosen file.
findings.title: Open file atomically to avoid symlink race after canonicalization

findings.body: The root directory is already canonicalized, but `root.join(name).canonicalize()` resolves the entire absolute path from scratch, repeating filesystem work for the root prefix on every call.
findings.failure_scenario: If `open_report` is called frequently or on deep directory trees, each invocation performs two full realpath-style traversals instead of one, increasing latency and filesystem load.
findings.title: Avoid re-resolving the canonical root for every candidate

findings.body: The change runs `report` through `sh -c` with a command string built by interpolating `user`. Any shell metacharacters in `user` (e.g., `;`, `&&`, backticks, or `$()`) are interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution. The original code passed `user` as a separate argument, which avoided shell interpretation. This change is also unrelated to the commit message about preserving report rows.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a user value such as `alice; rm -rf /`, causing the shell to execute `report --user alice; rm -rf /` and run arbitrary commands with the host privileges.
findings.title: Execute the report command with an argument list, not a shell

findings.body: `rows.sublist(1)` returns every element except the first, so the function no longer preserves the input list. It also throws a `RangeError` when `rows` is empty because the start index exceeds the list length.
findings.failure_scenario: When `renderReport` is called with an empty list, `rows.sublist(1)` throws `RangeError`; with any non-empty list, it silently omits the first row.
findings.title: Return the full rows list instead of dropping the first element

findings.anchor: test('returns rows', () async => expect(await renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']), isNotNull));
findings.body: The specification states "Rendering shall preserve every row." The previous test checked that renderReport returns the exact input rows, but the changed assertion only checks that the result is non-null. This allows implementations that drop, reorder, or alter rows to pass the test suite, breaking the spec contract.
findings.failure_scenario: An implementation returns an empty list or a list with different rows; the test passes because the result is non-null, so the regression is not caught and the report silently loses data.
findings.title: Restore the test that verifies rendering preserves every row

findings.body: The spec requires report commands to pass user names as arguments without a shell. The diff builds a shell command string with `final command = 'report --user $user';` and runs it through `sh -c`, which both violates the requirement and exposes the call to shell injection.
findings.failure_scenario: If `user` contains shell metacharacters such as `'; rm -rf /'`, the interpolated command string executes arbitrary commands via `sh -c`, leading to command injection.
findings.title: Pass user as a direct argument instead of interpolating into a shell command

findings.title: Return all rows instead of dropping the first one

findings.anchor: Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The method now returns Map.Entry<User, Integer> instead of User, and the timeout parameter changed from Integer to int and is no longer defaulted. Callers that previously received a User and could pass a null timeout will break at compile time or runtime. This contradicts the commit message 'preserve UserClient caller compatibility'.
findings.failure_scenario: Existing callers expecting User fetch(String, Integer) will fail to compile, and callers passing null for timeoutMs will now throw NullPointerException or a compile error because the parameter is now primitive int.
findings.suggestion: User fetch(String id, Integer timeoutMs) { return new User(id, timeoutMs == null ? 30000 : timeoutMs); }
findings.title: Return User instead of Map.Entry to preserve caller compatibility

findings.anchor: var user = new User(id, new Date().toGMTString());
findings.body: The removed ternary default (timeoutMs == null ? 30000 : timeoutMs) is no longer present, so callers that previously omitted a timeout by passing null will now fail. The new code also discards the timeout value by returning it unchanged in the entry, which does not preserve the original behavior of using the timeout for the User object.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invoking fetch(id, null) previously received a User with a 30000 ms timeout; now the call does not compile because timeoutMs is int, breaking backward compatibility.
findings.suggestion: var user = new User(id, timeoutMs == null ? 30000 : timeoutMs);
findings.title: Restore default timeout handling removed by refactor

findings.body: The return statement now returns Map.entry(user, timeoutMs), exposing an internal pair instead of the single User the original API returned. This changes the public method signature and breaks caller compatibility, contrary to the stated intent.
findings.title: Return User instead of Map.Entry to match original contract

findings.body: The previous implementation used repo.LoadMany(ids) to fetch all items in a single call. The new loop calls repo.Load(id) once per id, turning a batched lookup into N separate repository calls.
findings.failure_scenario: For a large ids slice, Enrich issues one repository call per id, increasing latency linearly with input size instead of the single batched lookup used previously.
findings.title: Batch item lookups instead of calling repo.Load per id

findings.body: ResultSliceFactory.Create returns an empty zero-capacity slice. Appending up to len(ids) items forces multiple slice reallocations and copies, which is inefficient for a change whose intent is an 'efficiency design'.
findings.failure_scenario: For large input slices, repeated append growth re-allocates and copies the backing array, increasing CPU and allocation pressure.
findings.title: Preallocate the result slice to avoid repeated growth

findings.body: The original Enrich returned every item loaded by repo.LoadMany(ids). The new loop only keeps items that are Active, have a non-nil Owner, and whose Owner is Enabled, silently omitting all other ids. Unless the contract intentionally changed to filter, callers expecting one result per input id will receive incomplete data.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller requests enrichment for an active item whose Owner is nil; Enrich returns a slice that does not contain that item, so downstream code may treat it as missing.
findings.title: Revisit Active/Owner.Enabled filtering that silently drops results

findings.body: The Active, Owner, and Enabled checks are nested three levels deep, making the loop body harder to scan than a single guard clause.
findings.title: Flatten nested conditions with guard clauses

findings.body: ResultSliceFactory is stateless and has a single caller; it only wraps the literal []Item{}. Delete the type and its Create method and use []Item{} directly at the call site.
findings.title: Remove unnecessary ResultSliceFactory

findings.body: Create is an exported method on an exported type introduced in this diff, yet it lacks a doc comment. Go convention requires a comment for every exported identifier.
findings.suggestion:

findings.body: The workflow now triggers on pull_request_target, which runs in the base repository and has access to secrets and write permissions. It then explicitly checks out the PR branch head SHA and runs npm test, executing arbitrary code from an external PR with base-repo privileges. This is the well-known pull_request_target + checkout code execution/exfiltration pattern.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker submits a PR that modifies package.json, a test file, or a dependency postinstall script to exfiltrate secrets or tamper with the repository; when the workflow runs, it checks out the attacker-controlled branch and executes npm test in the privileged base-repo context, leaking secrets or modifying repository state.
findings.title: Run PR checks in pull_request context instead of pull_request_target

findings.body: RELEASE_TOKEN is a secret with release privileges, but it is exported into the environment of npm test. Tests run code from dependencies and, because the PR head is checked out in a pull_request_target workflow, from the untrusted PR itself, making token exfiltration straightforward.
findings.failure_scenario: A compromised package or malicious PR test reads process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN and exfiltrates it, allowing unauthorized releases or privileged repository operations.
findings.title: Remove RELEASE_TOKEN from test job env

findings.body: In a pull_request_target workflow, actions/checkout defaults to the base repository ref for safety. Setting ref to github.event.pull_request.head.sha explicitly switches to the untrusted PR branch, enabling arbitrary code execution with base-repo privileges.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker-controlled PR branch contains malicious code in the checked-out files; npm test executes that code in the privileged base-repo context, allowing secret exfiltration or unauthorized repository changes.
findings.title: Remove explicit PR-head checkout ref

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: render_report now builds a shell command string by interpolating user_name directly and executes it with shell=True. Any shell metacharacters in user_name are interpreted by the shell, allowing arbitrary command execution. The previous list-form invocation avoided this by passing arguments directly.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes user_name containing shell metacharacters such as 'alice; rm -rf /', which subprocess.run passes to /bin/sh as 'report --user alice; rm -rf /', causing the shell to execute the attacker-supplied command and compromise the host.
findings.title: Pass command arguments as a list to avoid shell command injection

findings.body: The change constructs a shell command by interpolating user_name into a string and passes it to subprocess.run with shell=True. Any shell metacharacters in user_name (quotes, semicolons, backticks, $(), etc.) will be executed by the shell, leading to arbitrary command execution.
findings.failure_scenario: A user_name value such as 'alice; rm -rf /' or 'alice$(whoami)' is passed to render_report, causing the shell to execute the injected commands with the privileges of the running process.
findings.title: Fix shell injection via user_name interpolation

findings.body: The function previously returned the entire rows list, matching the expected behavior of preserving rows. The change returns rows[1:], silently discarding the first row without any documented reason. This is an off-by-one/boundary error that changes the contract of the function and can cause data loss for callers.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ['first', 'second'] expecting both rows back, but only receives ['second'], causing the first data row to be lost from any downstream processing or report output.
findings.title: Return full rows instead of dropping the first row

findings.body: The updated test only checks that render_report returns a non-None value, so a regression in the new rows[1:] slicing would not be caught. The test name also no longer describes the behavior being verified.
findings.failure_scenario: If render_report returns the full row list, an empty list, or the wrong tail, the test still passes, allowing a slicing regression to ship.
findings.title: Assert the actual sliced rows in render_report test

ground_truth.commit_message: feat: preserve report behavior while accepting user names

expected.label: replacement test no longer checks row preservation

findings.body: The function now returns a tuple instead of the original dictionary payload, and it uses datetime.utcnow(), which returns a naive datetime and is deprecated. The previous implementation returned an aware UTC datetime via datetime.now(UTC) and included timeout inside the dict. The import of UTC was also removed, so restoring the original behavior requires re-adding that import.
findings.failure_scenario: Consumers treating the return value as a dict raise TypeError on key access, and comparisons with timezone-aware datetimes raise TypeError because datetime.utcnow() is naive; Python 3.12+ also emits a deprecation warning for utcnow().
findings.title: Return the dict payload and use timezone-aware UTC datetime

findings.body: The UTC import was removed, leaving no timezone-aware helper in scope. Re-importing it allows datetime.now(UTC) to replace the deprecated datetime.utcnow().
findings.failure_scenario: Without UTC in scope, the fix for the deprecated utcnow() call cannot be applied, leaving the code with naive timestamps and future deprecation warnings.
findings.title: Import UTC to support timezone-aware timestamps

findings.body: The function derives the database identifier from PurePath(user_id).name, which collapses parent-directory references and path separators. An attacker can supply an identifier such as 'attacker/../victim' or '/victim' and the query will search for 'victim'. If the raw user_id is used for access-control checks, logging, or audit trails elsewhere, this normalization can bypass authorization and return another user's record. Remove the path normalization and use the original user_id directly; the parameterized query already prevents SQL injection.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker sends user_id='attacker/../victim'; upstream validation or audit logs see the raw string and allow the request, while find_user normalizes it to 'victim' and returns that user's row.
findings.title: Broken authorization: do not normalize user IDs with path operations

findings.body: The change uses PurePath(user_id).name to strip path-like separators from a user_id before binding it to a SQL parameter. This adds complexity and a misleading abstraction: user_id is not a filesystem path, and the database driver already handles parameter binding safely. The normalization is unrelated to the function's purpose and could mask invalid input rather than letting validation fail explicitly.
findings.failure_scenario: A user_id containing a slash (e.g. 'foo/bar') is silently truncated to 'bar', causing the query to match a different user than the caller intended.
findings.suggestion:
def find_user(connection, user_id: str):
    return connection.execute("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?", (user_id,)).fetchone()
findings.title: Remove needless PurePath normalization

findings.body: The userName argument is interpolated directly into a shell command string passed to execSync. If userName contains shell metacharacters such as spaces, quotes, semicolons, backticks, or $(), the attacker can execute arbitrary commands on the host. The original code used spawnSync with an separate argument array, which avoided invoking a shell and prevented injection.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker supplies a userName such as 'alice; rm -rf /' or 'alice$(whoami)', causing execSync to execute arbitrary shell commands with the privileges of the running process.
findings.title: Fix OS command injection in execSync call

findings.body: The function now returns rows.slice(1), which drops the first element. The original implementation returned the full rows array, and the test was weakened from checking equality to merely checking the result is defined, masking the data loss. Unless the contract intentionally changed to exclude the first row, this silently discards user data and breaks callers expecting all rows.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invoking renderReport('alice', ['first', 'second']) receives ['second'] instead of ['first', 'second'], causing reports to omit the first row without any error.
findings.title: Restore return of full rows array

findings.body: The test was changed from asserting the returned rows equal the input to asserting the result is merely defined. This weakened assertion no longer verifies the function returns the expected rows and would pass even if the function returned an wrong value, null, or an empty array. Combined with the new rows.slice(1) behavior, the test no longer catches data loss.
findings.failure_scenario: renderReport could return an incorrect or truncated result, and the test would still pass, allowing a regression to reach production.
findings.title: Restore meaningful test assertion

findings.body: The change builds a shell command by interpolating `userName` directly into the string passed to `execSync`, which runs through a shell. If `userName` ever contains shell metacharacters (spaces, quotes, semicolons, backticks, $(), etc.), the shell will parse and execute them, leading to arbitrary command execution. findings.failure_scenario: A userName value such as `'; rm -rf /; '` or `'$(malicious)'` is interpolated into the command string, the shell parses it as additional commands, and arbitrary code runs with the process privileges.

findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ['first', 'second'] and receives ['second'], so the first record is omitted from the rendered report.
findings.title: Return the full rows array instead of rows.slice(1)

findings.body: The test was weakened from an exact equality check to `.toBeTruthy()`, so it no longer verifies the actual return value. Because the implementation now returns `rows.slice(1)`, this test would pass even if the wrong subset of rows were returned.
findings.title: Assert the exact rows returned by renderReport

findings.body: The change imports execSync, which runs a command through a shell by default. Together with the interpolated command string, this violates the spec requirement that report commands shall not interpolate input into a shell.
findings.failure_scenario: A userName containing shell metacharacters is interpolated into the command string and executed by the shell when renderReport is called.
findings.title: Import spawnSync instead of execSync to avoid shell execution

findings.body: The previous implementation fetched all records in a single batch via repository.loadMany(ids). The new loop calls repository.load(id) once per id, sequentially, reintroducing an N+1 query pattern.
findings.failure_scenario: For a large ids array, the function performs one database round-trip per element, multiplying latency and likely exhausting the connection pool.
findings.title: Batch entity loads instead of issuing one query per id

findings.body: After awaiting repository.load(id), the code immediately reads item.active without checking whether item is null or undefined. If the repository returns a nullish value for an unknown id, the property access throws a TypeError and aborts enrichment for the remaining ids.
findings.failure_scenario: A request includes an id for which repository.load returns null; enrich throws an unhandled TypeError on item.active and fails the request instead of continuing with the remaining ids.
findings.suggestion:
const item = await repository.load(id);
    if (!item) continue;
findings.title: Skip null or undefined items returned by repository.load

findings.body: The code assumes every call to repository.load(id) returns an object with an active property. If load returns null, undefined, or a value without active, evaluating item.active throws a TypeError and aborts the entire enrichment.
findings.failure_scenario: When any id resolves to null/undefined or an object lacking active, enrich throws TypeError instead of returning a filtered array.
findings.title: Guard repository.load result before accessing properties

findings.body: The default value `timeoutMs = 30000` was removed, so callers that omit the argument now pass `undefined`. This breaks backward compatibility and contradicts the commit message claiming to preserve `fetchUser` compatibility.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invoking `fetchUser(123)` now passes `undefined` as `timeoutMs`, causing the returned value to contain `undefined` and any downstream timeout logic to misbehave.
findings.title: Restore the default timeoutMs value

findings.anchor: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toGMTString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.body: The function now returns a two-element array instead of the previous object, so callers reading `.id`, `.timeoutMs`, or `.fetchedAt` receive `undefined`. It also uses the deprecated `Date.prototype.toGMTString()`, which returns a different format than the previous `toISOString()`, further breaking consumers that parse ISO 8601 dates.
findings.failure_scenario: Existing code such as `const user = fetchUser(1); console.log(user.id, user.fetchedAt)` gets `undefined` for `user.id` and a GMT-formatted string instead of an ISO 8601 timestamp, causing runtime errors or incorrect behavior.
findings.suggestion: return { id, timeoutMs, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
findings.title: Return an object with an ISO timestamp

findings.body: The implementation now iterates over every element of `ids` and calls `repo.load` once per element, growing `results` with each match. If `ids` is large or `repo.load` performs I/O, this creates an N+1 query pattern and can exhaust CPU, memory, or downstream resources.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker can pass a very large `ids` slice to `enrich`, causing one repository load per element and a proportional memory allocation; if the repository is backed by a database or network service, this degrades or crashes the service.
findings.title: Batch repository loads to prevent denial of service

findings.body: The loop only pushes an item when `item.active` is true, `item.owner` is `Some(...)`, and `owner.enabled` is true. The previous implementation simply returned `repo.load_many(ids)`, which yields one entry per requested id, so this changes the function's contract and drops valid items without any signal to the caller.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ids for items that are inactive or have no/enabled=false owner; `enrich` returns a vector missing those items, causing downstream code to treat them as absent or to fail on the missing entries.
findings.title: Do not silently drop inactive or ownerless items

findings.body: The change replaces a single `repo.load_many(ids)` call with a loop that calls `repo.load(*id)` once per id. If `Repository` is backed by a database or network service, this introduces an N+1 query pattern that is slower and more resource-intensive than the original batch load, contradicting the 'rust-efficiency-design-v1' commit message.
findings.failure_scenario: For a large `ids` slice, the function issues one query per element instead of one batch query, increasing latency and load on the repository.
findings.title: Use the existing batch load instead of N+1 per-id queries

findings.body: The change replaces the batched repo.load_many(ids) with a loop that calls repo.load(*id) once per id, turning a single fetch into one fetch per input element so cost scales with ids.len().
findings.failure_scenario: When ids is large, enrich issues one repository round-trip per id, increasing latency, consuming connections, and potentially overwhelming the backend.
findings.title: Batch repository lookups instead of loading items one by one

findings.body: The `command` string interpolates `user` directly and is executed by `sh -c`, so shell metacharacters in `user` are interpreted as commands. findings.anchor: Future<List<Item>> enrich(List<String> ids, Repository repository) async {
findings.body: The change replaces repository.loadMany(ids) with an awaited loop that calls repository.load(id) for each input. That issues N+1 round-trips and silently filters out inactive items or items whose owner is null or disabled. If Repository still exposes loadMany, prefer a single batch call and apply the filtering explicitly afterward so callers can see which items are expected to be omitted.
findings.failure_scenario: A request with many ids becomes linearly slower, and callers that previously received one result per id now receive fewer items, causing missing data or downstream failures.
findings.title: Load IDs in batch instead of issuing sequential awaits

findings.body: The change replaces the batched repository.loadMany(ids) with an awaited repository.load(id) inside a loop, so every id now triggers its own repository round-trip. Cost scales linearly with ids.length and reintroduces N+1 behavior.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many values, enrich issues N sequential repository.load calls instead of one batch call, multiplying latency and connection usage.
findings.title: Batch item loads instead of issuing one query per id

findings.body: The loop body uses three levels of nested if statements to skip inactive items and items whose owner is missing or disabled. Early continues would make the happy path linear and reduce indentation.
findings.title: Flatten nested conditionals with guard clauses

findings.anchor: Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String id, int timeoutMs) {
findings.body: The method signature changed from `User fetch(String, Integer)` to `Map.Entry<User, Integer> fetch(String, int)`. This removes the previous stable `User` return contract and the null-to-30000-ms default, so existing callers expecting a `User` or passing `null` for timeout will fail to compile.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller such as `User u = client.fetch(id, null);` no longer compiles because the method now returns `Map.Entry` and requires a primitive `int`, breaking the build.
findings.title: Restore User return type and nullable Integer timeout parameter

findings.anchor: var statement = db.prepareStatement("SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ?");
findings.body: The method creates a PreparedStatement but never closes it. Because the ResultSet is returned to the caller, the statement stays open; if the caller only closes the ResultSet, the statement handle leaks. Over many calls this can exhaust database cursors or the connection/statement pool.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker or misbehaving client repeatedly calls find(); each leaked PreparedStatement consumes a database cursor or statement handle until the pool is exhausted and the application can no longer serve database requests.
findings.title: Close PreparedStatement to avoid resource exhaustion

findings.title: Guard userId before calling trim() and toLowerCase()

findings.body: The method creates a PreparedStatement but only returns the ResultSet. If the caller closes only the ResultSet, the PreparedStatement may remain open; if setString or executeQuery throws, the statement is leaked with no way for the caller to close it.

findings.title: Ensure PreparedStatement is closed with the ResultSet

findings.body: Enrich loops over the entire ids slice and issues one repository lookup per id with no length validation or upper bound. If the caller can supply an arbitrarily large slice, the function can generate an unbounded number of database queries.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker sends a request with a very large ids slice, causing Enrich to issue one repo.Load per id and consume excessive database connections or CPU, denying service to legitimate users.
findings.title: Limit ids slice size to prevent unbounded repository lookups

findings.body: The loop calls repo.Load(id) once per id, replacing the previous repo.LoadMany(ids). This is an classic N+1 pattern: each iteration issues a separate repository lookup, so the cost scales linearly with input size. If repo.LoadMany is still available, it should be used.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many elements, Enrich issues one repository round-trip per id, increasing latency and exhausting the underlying connection pool or resource budget.
findings.title: Batch item loading to avoid N+1 repository calls

findings.body: The original Enrich returned every item loaded for the supplied ids. The rewritten loop silently drops inactive items and any item whose Owner is nil or not Enabled. This changes the public result set and is not described in the commit message.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that previously received inactive items or items without an enabled owner now gets an empty or incomplete slice, causing missing data downstream.
findings.title: Explain or remove the new Active/Owner filter

findings.body: ResultSliceFactory is a struct with no state and a single method that just returns an empty slice. It is only used once, immediately instantiated, and its only purpose is to create an empty []Item. This is unnecessary indirection that adds a public symbol with no real utility.
findings.title: Remove unused ResultSliceFactory abstraction

findings.body: Create is a new exported method but has no doc comment, so godoc and callers have no description of what it returns.
findings.suggestion:
// Create returns a new empty []Item.
func (ResultSliceFactory) Create() []Item { return []Item{} }
findings.title: Add a doc comment for exported Create

findings.anchor: func FetchUser(id string, timeout time.Duration) (User, time.Duration) {
findings.body: FetchUser now reads a file named "defaults.json" from the current working directory using ioutil.ReadFile. The path is hardcoded but the function is part of a client package, so the file read is unconditional and the contents are discarded. This is an unsafe file access pattern: any file named defaults.json in the working directory is read on every call, and if the path were later made dynamic it would be a path traversal risk. More importantly, reading from disk in a getter-style function is unexpected and can expose arbitrary local files if the path is ever influenced by input. The ioutil package is also deprecated in favor of os.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker who can place or replace a file named defaults.json in the process working directory causes FetchUser to read and load attacker-controlled content; if the result were ever used, this could lead to information disclosure or code execution, and currently it performs unnecessary disk I/O that may leak file existence timing.
findings.title: Arbitrary file read via hardcoded path in FetchUser

findings.body: The workflow now triggers on pull_request_target, which runs in the base repository context and can access secrets and elevated permissions. It then checks out the pull request head commit and runs npm test, executing attacker-controlled code from forks with access to repository secrets. This is a pwn-request pattern.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious fork PR modifies package.json scripts so npm test exfiltrates secrets.RELEASE_TOKEN and writes back to the repository using the privileged workflow context.
findings.title: Replace pull_request_target trigger with pull_request

findings.body: The workflow uses `pull_request_target`, which runs in the base repository context and has access to secrets and a writable token. The added `actions/checkout` step explicitly checks out `${{ github.event.pull_request.head.sha }}`, so the job builds and runs untrusted code from the pull request with those privileges. This is the unsafe pattern GitHub warns against for `pull_request_target`.
findings.failure_scenario: A contributor opens a PR that modifies `package.json` test scripts or adds a postinstall hook; when the workflow runs, it checks out and executes that untrusted code with access to `secrets.RELEASE_TOKEN` and the repository token, allowing exfiltration or repository modification.
findings.title: Remove checkout of PR head under pull_request_target

findings.body: Exporting `secrets.RELEASE_TOKEN` as an environment variable for `npm test` exposes a sensitive credential to arbitrary code executed during tests. If the workflow processes untrusted PR code, the secret can be exfiltrated; even with trusted code, tests do not need release privileges. Remove the env block.
findings.failure_scenario: A compromised or malicious test dependency, or a fork PR, reads `process.env.RELEASE_TOKEN` during `npm test` and exfiltrates it.
findings.title: Do not pass release token into test step

findings.body: The validation only rejects the exact CIDR "0.0.0.0/0". Equivalent or other broad ranges such as "0.0.0.0/1", "128.0.0.0/1", or any public CIDR are accepted and applied directly to the SSH ingress rule. There is also no check that the value is a valid CIDR or belongs to an approved administrative network.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller sets admin_cidr = "0.0.0.0/1", which passes validation and causes aws_security_group_rule.admin to allow inbound TCP/22 from half of the IPv4 internet, exposing the instance to SSH brute-force attacks.
findings.title: Reject overly broad and public CIDRs for admin SSH access, not just 0.0.0.0/0

findings.body: The new `admin_cidr` variable is part of the module's public interface but has no `description`. Consumers and automated documentation tools cannot tell its purpose or expected format without reading the implementation.
findings.suggestion:
variable "admin_cidr" {
  description = "CIDR block allowed to reach the admin SSH security group rule."
findings.title: Add a description to the admin_cidr input variable

ground_truth.clean_trap: The ingress CIDR became configurable, but its safe default and validation explicitly reject public admin access.

findings.title: Remove IDOR risk from path-normalized user IDs

findings.body: The refactor removes the default value for timeoutMs and changes the return type from a single Record object to a tuple. Both alter the public API surface, so existing callers that omit timeoutMs or expect an object return will break, contradicting the commit message "retain fetchUser compatibility".
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that previously invoked fetchUser("1") without a timeout argument now gets a TypeScript compile-time error (or receives undefined for timeoutMs at runtime in plain JS), and any caller expecting a returned object must update to destructure a tuple.
findings.title: Keep fetchUser backward-compatible signature

findings.anchor: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toGMTString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.body: Date.toGMTString is deprecated and returns an RFC 1123/GMT date string (e.g., "Mon, 01 Jan 2024 00:00:00 GMT"), whereas the previous implementation used toISOString, which emits ISO 8601. Consumers parsing fetchedAt as ISO 8601 will fail or misparse the new format.
findings.failure_scenario: A downstream consumer parses fetchedAt with new Date(fetchedAt) or an ISO parser; the GMT string format causes Invalid Date or incorrect timestamp interpretation.
findings.suggestion: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.title: Use toISOString instead of deprecated toGMTString

findings.body: The change interpolates `userName` directly into a command string and executes it with `execSync`, which runs the string through a shell. If `userName` contains shell metacharacters such as `;`, `|`, backticks, or `$`, arbitrary commands can be executed. This change is also unrelated to the stated intent of keeping report output stable. Revert to `spawnSync` with an argument array and restore the `spawnSync` import.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes `userName = "alice; rm -rf /"`, causing `execSync` to run `report --user alice; rm -rf /` in the shell and execute the injected command.
findings.title: Avoid shell command injection when running the report tool

findings.body: `rows.slice(1)` removes the first element of `rows` before returning it. This changes the function's output and can silently drop data; for a single-row array it returns an empty array. This contradicts the prior behavior and the stated intent of keeping report output stable.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller invokes `renderReport("alice", ["header", "row1", "row2"])` expecting the full array and receives `["row1", "row2"]`, losing the first row.
findings.title: Return the full rows array instead of dropping the first row

findings.body: The updated test only checks that renderReport returns a truthy value, so it does not verify the new behavior of dropping the first row. A truthy assertion would pass even if the function returned the original array, a single string, or a wrong subset. The test name also no longer matches the actual assertion.
findings.title: Replace weak truthiness assertion with precise test for row slicing

findings.body: The change replaces spawnSync with execSync and interpolates userName directly into a shell command string. execSync invokes a shell by default, so any shell metacharacters in userName (spaces, quotes, semicolons, backticks, $(), etc.) will be interpreted by the shell. This is a command injection vulnerability. The previous spawnSync call passed userName as an array argument, which avoids shell interpretation.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes a malicious userName such as "bob; rm -rf /" or "bob$(whoami)", causing the shell to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the running process.
findings.title: Avoid shell injection via unsanitized user input in execSync

findings.body: The updated test only checks that renderReport returns a truthy value, so it does not verify the new behavior of dropping the first row. A truthy assertion would pass even if the function returned the original array, a single string, or an wrong subset. The test name also no longer matches the actual assertion.
findings.title: Replace weak truthiness assertion with precise test for row slicing

findings.body: The previous implementation used repository.loadMany(ids) to fetch all records in one batch call. The new for...of loop awaits repository.load(id) for each id sequentially, multiplying round-trips and increasing latency. The commit message "plant javascript-efficiency-design-v1" suggests an efficiency goal, so this structural change appears to move in the opposite direction.
findings.failure_scenario: For a list of N ids, enrich now performs N sequential asynchronous loads instead of one batch, increasing latency roughly linearly with N and raising load on the repository.
findings.title: Sequential per-item loads contradict efficiency-design intent

findings.body: The original enrich returned every item loaded for the supplied ids. The new code only pushes items that are active and have an owner whose enabled property is truthy. This silently drops inactive, ownerless, or disabled-owner records. The commit message only mentions planting a design pattern, not changing the result set, so this filtering is out of scope and may break callers expecting all ids enriched.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller that previously received inactive or unowned records in the returned array now gets an empty or smaller array, causing missing data downstream.
findings.title: Unannounced filtering changes enrich result set

findings.body: The previous implementation used repository.loadMany(ids), which fetches all requested items in a single round-trip. The new loop awaits repository.load(id) once per id, turning one batch call into N sequential calls.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids is large, the function issues one database or network round-trip per id, increasing latency linearly with input size and potentially exhausting the connection pool or hitting rate limits.
findings.title: Avoid N+1 queries by batching repository loads

findings.body: ResultArrayFactory.create() only ever returns a new empty array. It is a single-caller abstraction that adds indirection without encapsulating behavior, and its definition becomes dead code once the call site is simplified.
findings.title: Replace ResultArrayFactory with a plain array literal

findings.body: The function now returns an array `[{ id, fetchedAt }, timeoutMs]` instead of the previous object `{ id, timeoutMs, fetchedAt }`. This breaks any caller that destructures the return value as an object or accesses `.id`, `.timeoutMs`, or `.fetchedAt` on it. The commit claims to 'preserve fetchUser compatibility', but the return shape is changed incompatibly.
findings.failure_scenario: Existing callers such as `const user = fetchUser(1); user.fetchedAt` receive `undefined` and callers destructuring `const { id, timeoutMs } = fetchUser(1)` throw or get undefined values, causing runtime errors or silent failures.
findings.title: Return an object from fetchUser to preserve compatibility

findings.anchor: return [{ id, fetchedAt: new Date().toGMTString() }, timeoutMs];
findings.body: The default `timeoutMs = 30000` was removed, so callers omitting the second argument now pass `undefined` instead of 30000. Additionally, `toGMTString()` was substituted for `toISOString()`, changing the timestamp format from ISO 8601 to RFC 7231. Both changes contradict preserving compatibility.
findings.failure_scenario: Callers that omit `timeoutMs` receive `undefined` and consumers expecting an ISO 8601 timestamp from `fetchedAt` fail to parse the GMT string, breaking downstream logic.
findings.suggestion: return { id, timeoutMs, fetchedAt: new Date().toISOString() };
findings.title: Restore the default timeout and ISO timestamp format

required timeout and array return break compatibility intent

findings.body: The loop only pushes an item when `item.active` is true, `item.owner` is `Some(...)`, and `owner.enabled` is true. The previous implementation simply returned `repo.load_many(ids)`, which yields one entry per requested id, so this changes the function's contract and drops valid items without any signal to the caller.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ids for items that are inactive or have no/enabled=false owner; `enrich` returns a vector missing those items, causing downstream code to treat them as absent or to fail on the missing entries.
findings.title: Do not silently drop inactive or ownerless items

findings.body: The loop calls repo.load once per id, replacing the previous batched repo.load_many(ids). This reintroduces an N+1 query pattern: the cost scales linearly with ids.len().
findings.failure_scenario: For a large ids slice, enrich issues one repository query per id instead of a single batched query, increasing latency and exhausting the connection pool.
findings.title: Batch repository lookups instead of loading one item per loop iteration

findings.body: `VecFactory::create` only delegates to `Vec::new()`, adding an empty abstraction that does not improve efficiency and is inconsistent with the 'rust-efficiency-design-v1' commit message. Pre-allocating capacity matching the input size is a concrete efficiency improvement.
findings.title: Replace VecFactory with a capacity-reserved vector

findings.body: The loop body nests three levels of checks (item.active, item.owner existence, owner.enabled) before pushing an item. Using early continue statements for inactive items, missing owners, and disabled owners would reduce indentation and make the push unconditional.
findings.title: Flatten nested filter conditions with guard clauses

findings.body: VecFactory is a private struct whose only method returns Vec::new, and enrich is its only caller. It adds no behavior and can be deleted in favor of the standard library constructor.
findings.title: Remove the VecFactory wrapper struct

findings.body: The sandbox relies on std::fs::canonicalize to ensure the resolved path is under root, but canonicalize validates path strings, not inodes. An attacker who can create a hard link inside the report directory to a sensitive file elsewhere on the same filesystem will produce a canonical path that is still under root, so the strip_prefix check passes and the target file is opened. Use O_NOFOLLOW and verify the opened file's identity (for example via fstat and /proc/self/fd), or ensure the report directory is not attacker-writable.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker creates a hard link /reports/secret pointing to /etc/shadow; canonicalize returns /reports/secret, strip_prefix succeeds, and File::open returns the contents of /etc/shadow.
findings.title: Canonicalize-based path check is bypassable via hard links

findings.body: The code canonicalizes the candidate path and checks that it is under root, then calls File::open(candidate) in a separate step. Because the filesystem can change between canonicalize and open, an attacker who controls the report directory can swap the validated path for a symlink to a file outside root, causing File::open to follow the symlink and read arbitrary files. Open the file atomically relative to a held directory file descriptor (for example with openat) instead of validating a path and then reopening it.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker creates a regular file at the requested report path; after canonicalize confirms it is under root, they replace it with a symlink to /etc/passwd before File::open runs; the function returns the sensitive file.
findings.title: Fix time-of-check/time-of-use race when opening reports

findings.body: When name resolves outside root, the function returns PermissionDenied if the target exists but NotFound if it does not, because canonicalize fails before the strip_prefix check. If callers expose the error kind, an attacker can probe for files outside the sandbox by comparing error kinds. Return a uniform error for any disallowed path, or validate the name before canonicalizing it.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker calls open_report with name ../etc/passwd and then ../etc/nonexistent; the first returns PermissionDenied and the second NotFound, revealing that /etc/passwd exists.
findings.title: Do not leak file existence through error kinds

ground_truth.clean_trap: An untrusted name is joined to a root, but both paths are canonicalized and strip_prefix enforces containment before opening.

findings.body: The change builds a shell command by interpolating the `user` parameter into a string and runs it via `sh -c`. This allows shell metacharacters in `user` to be interpreted and execute arbitrary commands. The previous implementation passed `user` as a separate argument to `Process.run`, which keeps the value in argv and prevents injection.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker passes a `user` value containing shell metacharacters such as `'; malicious_command #`; the shell parses it as part of the command string and executes `malicious_command` with the host process's privileges.
findings.title: Avoid OS command injection by passing arguments as a list

findings.body: The function now iterates over every id in the caller-supplied ids list and awaits repository.load(id) sequentially. There is no validation of ids.length or a maximum batch size, so an attacker can pass an arbitrarily large list to cause excessive CPU, memory, and I/O consumption, leading to denial of service.
findings.failure_scenario: An attacker sends a request with a very large ids list; each id triggers a separate repository.load await, keeping the isolate busy and consuming resources until the loop finishes or the process is exhausted.
findings.title: Limit the number of IDs processed in the sequential loop

findings.body: The original enrich returned one item for every id via repository.loadMany. The replacement only adds items that are active and have a non-null, enabled owner. If this filtering is not intentional, callers will receive fewer results than requested with no indication that items were dropped.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller requesting enrichment for a list of ids receives a shortened list for inactive or ownerless items and treats the missing ids as not found, breaking one-result-per-id expectations.
findings.title: Document or remove the new active/owner filtering

findings.anchor: Future<List<Item>> enrich(List<String> ids, Repository repository) async {
findings.body: The change replaces the single repository.loadMany(ids) call with a loop that awaits repository.load(id) once per id. Each iteration now incurs its own repository round-trip, so latency scales linearly with the size of ids and the previously batched path is lost.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids contains many entries, enrich issues one repository round-trip per id, multiplying latency and potentially exhausting the connection pool, whereas the original implementation fetched all items in a single batch.
findings.title: Batch item loads to avoid N+1 repository round-trips

findings.body: The change trims and lowercases the user-provided `userId` before querying the database. This silently changes the lookup key, so a request for ' Alice ' or 'ALICE' will be treated as 'alice'. If the stored IDs are case-sensitive or preserve whitespace, this will fail to find valid users or, worse, return the wrong user when IDs differ only in case. It also means the function no longer returns what callers expect for the exact ID they passed, breaking the contract of a lookup by ID.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes the exact user ID 'Alice' stored in the database; the function lowercases it to 'alice', the query finds no match, and the user is incorrectly reported as missing.

findings.title: Do not silently mutate user IDs before database lookup

findings.body: The render method now constructs a shell command by concatenating the user parameter directly into /bin/sh -c. Because user is a method argument, it should be treated as untrusted input; shell metacharacters such as semicolons, backticks, or $() are interpreted by /bin/sh, allowing arbitrary command execution. findings.body: The original implementation returned every item loaded for the supplied ids. The new code only adds items that are active, have a non-null owner, and have an enabled owner. Unless this filtering is the intended new contract, callers will receive fewer items than they requested.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller passes ids for items that are inactive or have disabled/no owners and receives an incomplete list, causing downstream processing to miss records.
findings.title: Document or remove unexplained filtering of inactive or unowned items

findings.body: The original Enrich returned one item for every input id. The rewritten function only appends results when item.Active is true, item.Owner is non-nil, and item.Owner.Enabled is true. This silently omits inactive items and items without an enabled owner, changing the function's contract and likely causing missing-data errors for callers that still expect all requested ids to be returned.
findings.failure_scenario: A caller requests ids that include an inactive item or an item whose owner is disabled; Enrich returns a shorter slice missing that item, so downstream code treats it as deleted or fails with a not-found error.
findings.title: Review unexplained Active/Owner filtering that drops requested items

findings.body: The loop calls repo.Load(id) once per id, replacing the previous batched repo.LoadMany(ids). This is an classic N+1 pattern: the cost scales linearly with input size and loses any batching the repository could perform.
findings.failure_scenario: When ids is large, Enrich issues one repository load per id instead of a single batched load, increasing latency, connection usage, and load on the backing store.
findings.title: Batch the per-id repository loads

findings.body: The workflow switches the trigger to pull_request_target, which runs in the base repository context and has access to secrets. It then explicitly checks out github.event.pull_request.head.sha and runs npm test, executing arbitrary code from the PR branch with that privileged context. This is the well-known dangerous use of pull_request_target and allows an external contributor to exfiltrate secrets or pivot through the repository.
findings.failure_scenario: A malicious PR changes the test script or a test file; when the workflow runs it checks out the PR head and executes npm test, giving that code access to repository secrets such as RELEASE_TOKEN and the ability to publish releases or modify source.
findings.title: Use pull_request instead of pull_request_target for untrusted PR builds

findings.body: Checking out github.event.pull_request.head.sha under pull_request_target causes the job to run attacker-controlled code from the pull request while still holding base-repository privileges and secrets. The default checkout for pull_request_target is the base branch; overriding it to the PR head removes that protection.
findings.failure_scenario: An external PR modifies package scripts or test files; the workflow checks out the PR head and executes npm test, running the attacker's code with access to RELEASE_TOKEN and base-repo write permissions.
findings.title: Remove explicit checkout of PR head in pull_request_target workflow

findings.body: RELEASE_TOKEN is injected into the environment of npm test, which runs code from an untrusted pull request under pull_request_target. The token is unnecessary for running tests and exposes a credential that can publish releases or perform other privileged operations. The workflow-level permissions: contents: read restriction does not apply to custom secrets.
findings.failure_scenario: Any code executed during npm test — including a compromised dependency or a malicious PR test file — can read RELEASE_TOKEN from the environment and use it to create releases or push artifacts.
findings.title: Remove RELEASE_TOKEN from the test job environment

expected.label: pull_request_target executes untrusted head with a secret

findings.body: Using a floating major version tag for a third-party action in a workflow that has pull-request write permissions creates a supply-chain risk. If the v6 tag is retargeted to a malicious commit, the workflow will execute it with a write-capable GITHUB_TOKEN. Pin the action to a specific commit SHA and optionally add a version comment.
findings.failure_scenario: If the actions/labeler@v6 tag is compromised and retargeted to malicious code, every triggered run executes that code with a GITHUB_TOKEN that can write pull requests, allowing unauthorized labeling or further repository access.
findings.title: Pin actions/labeler to a commit SHA

findings.body: The validation rule only rejects the literal CIDR 0.0.0.0/0. It does not prevent other public or overly broad CIDRs (e.g., 0.0.0.0/1, 1.0.0.0/8, 128.0.0.0/1, or any public IP range) from being assigned to admin_cidr. Since this variable controls SSH ingress to the admin security group, a user can still open port 22 to the public internet or large swaths of it while passing validation.
findings.failure_scenario: A user sets admin_cidr to 0.0.0.0/1 or a public /8, validation passes, and the security group rule exposes SSH to broad public networks, allowing brute-force and unauthorized access attempts.
findings.title: CIDR validation only blocks 0.0.0.0/0, not all public ranges

findings.body: The new `admin_cidr` variable is a public module input but has no `description`; users of this module cannot discover its purpose or intended use from the interface.
findings.title: Add a description to the admin_cidr variable
